description: We are a team of motivated high school students with a strong interest in computer science, artificial intelligence, and innovative problem-solving. Our team brings experience in programming, software development, AI-powered tools, and collaborative projects. We are passionate about using technology to address real-world challenges and exploring creative solutions through NASA's open data and resources.
summary:
With Prometheus Torch, anyone can access historical wildfire information from around the globe, regardless of whether they have expertise in the area or not. 

The MODIS system was capturing data for 2 decades but is being replaced with VIIRS. However, VIIRS captures about 3.7 times as many hotspots which can make it seem like a significant increase in the amount of burning. 

By converting VIIRS and MODIS data to common measurements, we bridge the gap for fire planners, researchers, and reporters. Prometheus Torch also allows users to check a fire calendar that outlines months with peak fire activity, as well as indicators that inform them how much fire activity is typically expected.
details:
Prometheus Torch can analyse and compare global historical wildfires. We have calibrated our project to allow us to compare VIIRS fire cell-days to Aqua equivalent values using MODIS Aqua as a reference. This allows us to easily compare the amount of burning across different systems. In Brazil the raw VIIRS data suggests burning rose about 60% per decade, but the harmonized record shows it fell about 34% per decade.

Our program has been designed to have an easy to use visual interface and has clear scientific methodology. This allows the user to explore the data and see the evidence behind the results. 

The interactive map has a guided tutorial and contains easy to understand data and analytics for all global data. It also shows “Critical weeks”, the fewest weeks that hold 80% of a typical year’s burning, and whether the season has shifted. The aim of our project was to help students, researchers and members of the public understand satellite data better.

We hid one year at a time and predicted it from the other satellite. For the US, weekly error was 0.12 with our method versus 1.71 for uncorrected VIIRS. We built a simulated region with a planted trend of +12.5% per decade. The pipeline recovered +12.5%, while the raw record overstated it at 44%. We publish every test, including ones where our method did not beat a simpler baseline.

Our program was created using Python to process and analyse our data, JavaScript and React to create our website and data from NASA FIRMS satellites. During development we have used OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. Our program has been creatively designed to link the calibration of the satellites with an interactive explanation to allow the user to understand the trends.

We have taken into account sensor differences, missing data, uncertainties, accessibility and clarity. Hotspots are areas detected by the satellite that are hot, they are not individual wildfires. The results do not directly relate to burned area or damage. The current analysis uses day time data that may not always be available depending on the satellite and location. In the future, we could add night time analysis that has been validated individually and more recent data when reliable data becomes available.
